title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Residents gather signatures to recall Springfield Twp supervisor over data center approvals.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Monday, September 7, and residents in one Oakland County township are already moving to change who decides these projects.
That's right — the big story today is the recall push against Springfield Township supervisor Ric Davis.
Yesterday, residents started gathering signatures to oust him, blaming the supervisor for fast-tracking data center projects that could strain local roads, power, and water.
Why target him specifically, Graham? What's the history here?

Davis has been the supervisor pushing for a careful approach. Back in December 2025 the township board passed a 180-day moratorium on data center applications to study impacts and write new zoning rules.
So he's trying to slow things down, yet residents see it as fast-tracking? That tension feels familiar across the state.

Exactly. A developer had already expressed interest in an 84-acre site near Andersonville Road for two or three large buildings. Davis met with them but stressed the township has no municipal water or sewer and would halt anything risking natural resources.
How does this fit into the bigger pattern of recalls we've seen?

Bridge Michigan tracked at least 28 officials in eight communities facing recalls tied to data center decisions. In Saline Township, officials dealt with recalls over an OpenAI-Oracle project after settling a lawsuit. Augusta Township had a full board targeted after rezoning farmland.
So this isn't isolated. What does a successful recall actually change for future projects?
It would shift control of the board and any future approvals. Voters could elect someone with a different stance on tax breaks, environmental reviews, or outright bans.
And the stakes for residents go way beyond one township. We're talking electric bills, right?

Yes. Data centers can pull hundreds of megawatts — enough to power tens of thousands of homes. That demand can push up regional rates, especially when utilities like DTE and Consumers Energy are already negotiating gigawatts of new commitments.
Water use is another big one. These facilities often need millions of gallons a day for cooling.
Right, and many rural townships like Springfield don't have the infrastructure. That forces tough choices about wells, aquifers, and whether to extend service from neighboring systems.
Farmland is getting converted too. How many acres are we talking about statewide?
Proposals have targeted hundreds of acres in places like Augusta and Saline. Once rezoned industrial, that land is hard to bring back for agriculture.
What happens next with the signatures in Springfield?
Organizers need enough valid signatures from township voters to trigger a recall election. If they succeed, it goes to the ballot and could reshape the board before more projects advance.
Meanwhile other communities are hitting pause too. Let's move to quick hits.
Ypsilanti is keeping its data center freeze in place while studying power and water impacts. The moratorium blocks large projects for now.
That could ripple out to Ann Arbor and beyond on electricity rates if approvals come later.
In Saline Township, supervisors delayed a vote on a 12-year tax break for the big Oracle campus. Residents are questioning the revenue loss versus promised jobs.
A developer is restarting plans to turn the old Emerson Electric site into a data center, bringing new power demand questions.
Over in western Mason County, two major data centers broke ground on Saturday — big electricity draw and construction jobs on the way.
Kalamazoo added a moratorium to its zoning code to slow the rush while it studies impacts.
Garfield Township in Grand Traverse County is taking a full year to craft rules on noise, water, and power.
A university town hall in mid-Michigan gave residents their first concrete look at megawatt and water-use numbers for proposed projects.
Lakeshore Township is blocking data centers with existing zoning that keeps them away from homes and wells.
And Ypsilanti-area activists are planning a protest Saturday over water use at two proposed campuses.
Now let's look at what's on deck for listeners who want to weigh in.
Tomorrow, September 9, the City of Ionia has an informational meeting on the data center industry and local considerations.
Also on the 9th, University of Michigan is hosting a town hall on the proposed high-performance computing facility in Ypsilanti Township.
And on September 15, Ypsilanti City Council holds a public hearing on zoning changes and the 60-day emergency moratorium.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.
Thanks for listening.

episode_title: Recall Effort Targets Springfield Supervisor Amid Data Center Pushback
